form.intro: This is the filing form as we have it so far. A value appears only where something you gave us backs it — everything else stays marked to be supplied rather than guessed.
form.title: The filing form
help.amount_bracket: Which side of the thresholds your budget falls on. Answering this settles your class without naming a figure.
help.amount_bracket.example: Under ¥300,000 is three-class; ¥800,000 or more is one-class
help.episode_count: How many episodes the finished series has. An estimate is fine; it does not affect which class you are in.
help.episode_minutes: Length of a single episode, in minutes. This decides whether the work counts as a micro-drama at all: twenty minutes or more and it follows a different path.
help.genre_keywords: A few words for the genre, separated by commas. Used alongside the logline when checking subject matter.
help.investment_amount_rmb: The total investment in RMB, digits only. Your budget range already decides your class — this exact figure is what the filing form itself asks for.
help.logline: One or two sentences on what happens. This is what gets checked against the sensitive-subject rules, so describe the plot rather than the mood.
help.logline.example: An undercover officer infiltrates a trafficking ring and risks being exposed.
help.no_clauses: The hint above is all the policy library has for this field. It comes from NRTA Circular 35 (2024), which isn't in the snapshot as a citable clause yet.
help.platform_promoted: Tick only if a platform has agreed to feature the work — sponsor-promoted, or placed on a home or landing screen. This usually gets settled after the film is made, so leave it unticked if no deal exists yet.
help.platform_promoted.example: unticked, unless you already have the agreement
help.production_stage: How far the work has got. It decides what we ask you next — and it matters to the rules too, because a one-class project must be filed before production starts.
help.synopsis: A paragraph on the story — this is the plot summary the filing form asks for, and it is what the subject check reads. Write it the way you would describe the show to a friend; the check has to quote your own words back to you, so plain description works better than a pitch.
help.synopsis.example: Two old friends reunite in a small town; one is drawn into an anti-narcotics operation and his cover starts to slip.
help.title: What you're calling it for now. It doesn't have to be final, but the filing form needs a title, so an empty one comes back as a gap later.
help.unavailable: The model isn't configured, so I can only show the hint above.
help.voluntary_key_declaration: Tick to declare the work as a key micro-drama by choice. It means the strictest route, in exchange for a distribution licence — worth it for awards, priority scheduling and negotiating with platforms.
home.does.class: Tells you which of the three classes your project falls in, and shows you the clause it read to decide.
home.does.form: Fills in the filing form from what you have given it, and locks a copy so the version reviewed is provably the one you approved.
home.does.route: Tells you who you file with, whether you must file before you start, and whether you can publish while you wait.
home.does.script: Reads your script against the same rules and points at the passages most likely to be questioned.
home.lede: Chinese micro-dramas have to be filed with the authorities before they go out, and which rules apply to you depends on your subject and your budget. This works out which ones, and gets your paperwork ready — so nothing comes as a surprise after you have spent the money.
home.not.advice: It is a pre-check, not legal advice. It shows you the rule it applied so you can check it yourself.
home.not.guess: It does not invent facts. Anything it cannot read from your files or your answers is left visibly blank rather than filled with a plausible guess.
home.not.submit: It never submits anything. A filing is made by a licensed company, and that stays a decision you make with a person.
home.title: Before you file your micro-drama

length.verdict.web_film: At 20 minutes or more it stops being a micro-drama and becomes a web film — a different set of rules, and not the ones this tool checks. Article 2 draws the line there.

wizard.intent.intro: A few questions, then we tell you which class your project falls in, who it files with, and what you have to do. Nothing here is submitted anywhere — it is a pre-check, not legal advice, and it never files on your behalf.
wizard.intent.title: Tell us about the project
wizard.key_conditions_guidance: Leave both unticked unless you already know otherwise. Platform promotion is a commercial arrangement usually settled after the film is made, and declaring voluntarily is a choice to take the strictest route in exchange for a distribution licence — useful for awards, priority scheduling and negotiating with platforms.
wizard.key_conditions_note: Either of these makes a project a key micro-drama on its own, whatever the investment amount — NRTA Circular 35 (2024).
wizard.more_conditions: Two more things that can make it a key micro-drama
wizard.platform_promoted: Platform will feature it (sponsor-promoted, or shown on a home or landing screen)
wizard.stage_hint.idea: Then we only need the story and a rough length. The budget comes later, when you actually know it — and we will show you what each level would mean before you decide.
wizard.stage_hint.production_complete: We will check the script against the rules and point you at the specific scenes worth reviewing in your finished cut.
wizard.stage_hint.script_ready: Good — upload the script on the next screen and we will read the episode count, running time and synopsis out of it rather than making you type them again.
wizard.stage_hint.unknown: Answer what you can and leave the rest. Anything unknown stays unknown, and we assume the stricter class until you tell us otherwise.
